notes: C01's own instruction, read from /mnt/project-files/chatgpt-stress-test-answers-2026-09-22/connection-answers.json: 'Do not migrate a working 13/127 pack back wholesale merely because the research grouping used 14/92; reconcile subjects/IDs with the existing crosswalk and keep useful content.' So this is a reconciliation, not an append and not a replacement.

THE HAZARD THAT MAKES THIS BIGGER THAN IT LOOKS. Two packs now key into this vocabulary, not one. us-state-and-local declares the domains and issues; us-policy-positions declares 66 authored positions that reference those issues by qualified stable key. Renaming or splitting a domain changes the domainId on its issues, and re-keying an issue strands every position pointing at it. A crosswalk that accounts for only the sourced pack will silently orphan authored content, and because the loader rejects an unresolvable reference by name rather than throwing, it will look like a clean load with fewer positions in it. Any crosswalk has to be checked against BOTH packs and against the loaded proposition count.

Not urgent in the sense that nothing is broken: the shipped 13/127 vocabulary loads with zero rejections and carries positions in every domain. This is about doing the reconciliation correctly whenever it is taken.
question: The returned policy taxonomy groups state and local policy into fourteen domains across ninety-two items; the vocabulary shipped and loading today is thirteen domains across a hundred and twenty-seven issues, chosen because only that grouping carried issue rows and its groupings matched referral practice. For each of the fourteen domains, which of the thirteen does it correspond to — the same thing renamed, a split of one, a merge of several, or genuinely absent from the thirteen? And for the ninety-two items, which of the hundred and twenty-seven does each map to, naming the items that have no counterpart and the issues that would be lost if the ninety-two replaced them? A rename, a split and an addition have different consequences for identifiers already in use, so say which each one is rather than giving a list.

sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Carries the thirteen domains and a hundred and twenty-seven issues as shipped, each issue with the levels that ordinarily decide it. It records the reasoning for choosing thirteen over fourteen at the time, but predates the returned answer and maps nothing onto it.

States the thirteen-versus-fourteen reconciliation and the hedge taken at the time — elections, ethics, libraries, arts and parks were given their own issue keys so a later split would not need to invent them. It names the hedge; it does not establish what the fourteenth domain is.

Sixty-six authored positions keyed to the sourced issues by qualified stable key. It is the reason a crosswalk cannot be applied to the sourced pack alone, and it says nothing about which mapping is right.

title: Crosswalk the shipped thirteen-domain vocabulary against the returned fourteen
usableAnswer: A row per returned domain naming its counterpart among the thirteen and the KIND of relationship — identical, renamed, split from, merged into, or new — and the same for items against issues, with both directions of unmatched entries listed explicitly. Enough that the mapping can be applied as a rename table rather than as a judgement call, and enough that every currently shipped issue key can be checked for whether it survives.
whyItMatters: The vocabulary is the thing every bill, every position and eventually every conviction is keyed to, so its identifiers are load-bearing in a way most content is not. Getting the reconciliation wrong does not produce an error; it produces a quieter game, with positions that no longer attach to anything and a loader that reports a clean load. Doing it once, from a mapping rather than from a reading, is the difference.
